claims.claim: Of ten common study techniques, only practice testing and distributed (spaced) practice earn a high-utility rating; interleaving, self-explanation and elaborative interrogation are moderate; rereading, highlighting, summarising, keyword mnemonics and imagery are low.
claims.source_title: Improving Students' Learning With Effective Learning Techniques: Promising Directions From Cognitive and Educational Psychology
claims.key_numbers: 10 techniques rated; 2 high utility (practice testing, distributed practice), 3 moderate (elaborative interrogation, self-explanation, interleaved practice), 5 low; effect sizes not shown in search summary
claims.implication: The two techniques the skills already lean on (retrieval starters/exit tickets, spaced re-tests for examready) are the right ones; the Spanish Flashcards and Shooting Gallery are practice testing and should stay central. Anything in the maths 'teach 30-40 min' block that amounts to re-reading notes or highlighting should be replaced with worked examples plus self-explanation prompts, and the Spanish app should not add keyword-mnemonic features.

claims.claim: Spreading retrieval of the same material across separate sessions beats retrieving it repeatedly in one session by a large margin, but making the gaps grow (expanding schedule) is no better than keeping them equal.
claims.source_title: A Meta-Analytic Review of the Benefit of Spacing out Retrieval Practice Episodes on Retention
claims.key_numbers: 29 studies; 39 effect sizes (subset 1) and 54 (subset 2); spaced vs massed retrieval g = 0.74; expanding vs uniform schedule reported as non-significant g = 0.034 in a secondary search summary (verify against paper). Kang, Lindsey, Mozer & Pashler 2014 likewise found expanding and equal-interval retrieval equivalent at an 8-week test.
claims.implication: The tracker's review_queue should guarantee that each secure or developing topic is retrieved again in a later session, not just more times in the same session; the two-full-sessions-on-one-day pattern (2 Sep) forfeits most of this benefit. There is no need to build an SM-2-style expanding scheduler: a simple rule such as 'retest each topic roughly every 2-4 weeks' captures the effect.

claims.claim: In mathematics specifically, spacing practice across sessions gives a reliable but smaller benefit than in other subjects, and the benefit of quiz-style retrieval over restudy has not been shown to be robust for maths material.
claims.source_title: A Meta-analytic Review of the Effectiveness of Spacing and Retrieval Practice for Mathematics Learning
claims.key_numbers: Spaced vs massed: g = 0.28 (27 studies, 53 effect sizes); isolated learning g = 0.43, course-embedded g = 0.24; testing vs restudy g = 0.18 with 95% CI crossing zero
claims.implication: For maths the lever is spaced problem-solving practice, not flashcard-style recall of facts: the 10-minute starter should be old-topic problems drawn from the review queue (as the 4 Sep plan already does with A4 and HCF/LCM), and the skill should not substitute 'quiz her on the rule' for 'give her a problem'. Expect modest gains per topic and plan more cycles rather than fewer.

claims.claim: Seventh-grade pupils (the same age as this student) who did mixed-topic maths assignments over four months scored 61% versus 38% for blocked practice on a surprise test a month later.
claims.source_title: A randomized controlled trial of interleaved mathematics practice
claims.key_numbers: 787 students, 54 grade-7 classes, 5 schools, 4 months; unannounced test 1 month later: interleaved 61% vs blocked 38%, d = 0.83, 95% CI [0.68, 0.97]. Earlier RCT (Rohrer, Dedrick & Stershic 2015, 126 seventh graders) found the heavier interleaved dose scored higher at 1-day and 1-month delays; percentages not shown in search summary.
claims.implication: The 30-minute practise block should mix problem types so that no two consecutive questions use the same method, forcing her to choose the method from the problem, which is exactly what a GCSE paper demands and what the 'answer-targeting' habit undermines. Interleaved sets also space earlier topics automatically, so the tracker could log which topics each practice run touched (it already allows topic refs per item).

claims.claim: Across all interleaving studies the benefit is moderate, and for mathematical tasks it is small-to-moderate; interleaving helps most when the mixed items are similar and easily confused.
claims.source_title: Similarity matters: A meta-analysis of interleaved learning and its moderators
claims.key_numbers: 59 studies, 238 effect sizes, 158 samples; overall g = 0.42; mathematical tasks g = 0.34; visual materials g = 0.67; words g = -0.39 (blocking better)
claims.implication: Interleave confusable pairs deliberately: HCF with LCM, mean with median, area with perimeter, expected with relative frequency (P2-P3), and the recurring sign-error/collecting-terms sub-skill (A4) mixed with expanding brackets. For Spanish vocabulary the words finding cautions that pure word lists may be better learned in blocks first, then mixed in the Shooting Gallery once known.

claims.claim: Practice tests improve learning more than restudying and more than every other comparison condition, with the size of the gain depending on test format, feedback and study features.
claims.source_title: Rethinking the Use of Tests: A Meta-Analysis of Practice Testing
claims.key_numbers: Overall effect size not shown in search summary; a Learning Scientists summary describes it as covering 217 studies; effects moderated by practice-test features, participant characteristics, outcome constructs and methodology
claims.implication: Keeps the starter and exit-ticket structure justified across both subjects; the exact magnitude should be taken from the Yang et al. 2021 classroom meta-analysis (C7) rather than this one because its overall figure could not be confirmed.

claims.claim: Low-stakes quizzing in real classrooms raises achievement by a medium amount, and the gain is larger when corrective feedback is given, when the quiz format matches the final test, and when the same material is tested more than once.
claims.source_title: Testing (quizzing) boosts classroom learning: A systematic and meta-analytic review
claims.key_numbers: 222 independent studies, 48,478 students; g = 0.499; moderators include provision of corrective feedback, test format consistency, material matching, number of test repetitions, treatment duration
claims.implication: Exit tickets should be exam-format (written working, marks per question, calculator/non-calculator labelled) with immediate corrective feedback, not a chat quiz; the two practice questions 'not submitted before the session ended' lost both the retrieval and the feedback. The tracker could record whether each practice item received feedback and count repetitions per topic across sessions, which the current status rules do not capture.

claims.claim: The best gap between first learning and a review is roughly 10-20% of the time until the test when the test is weeks away, shrinking to about 5% when the test is a year away.
claims.source_title: Spacing effects in learning: A temporal ridgeline of optimal retention
claims.key_numbers: Over 1,350 participants; gaps up to 3.5 months; final test up to 1 year later; optimum gap about 20% of test delay for delays of a few weeks, falling to about 5% at one year
claims.implication: With the maths exam about 250 days away (4 Sep 2026 to 14 May 2027) the evidence-supported review gap is roughly 12-50 days; for the Dec 2026 mock (~100 days) it is 5-20 days. The tracker's 'examready after a re-test at least 3 weeks after securing' sits inside this band, but the 'ageing after 8 weeks untouched' flag is at the far edge: the eight ageing topics (N1-N3, N16, A1-A3, R1-R3) should be re-tested now and secure topics touched every 3-6 weeks, not 8.

claims.claim: The efficient dose is to practise each new item until it has been recalled correctly three times in the first session, then relearn it to one correct recall in about three later, widely spaced sessions.
claims.source_title: Optimizing schedules of retrieval practice for durable and efficient learning: how much is enough?
claims.key_numbers: 533 students; over 100,000 hand-scored recall responses; initial criterion 1-4 correct recalls, then 1-5 relearning sessions; prescription = 3 correct recalls then 3 relearning sessions. Janes, Dunlosky, Rawson & Jasnow 2020 applied this 'successive relearning' in a real course: at least 10% higher exam performance, effect sizes 0.54 to 1.10.
claims.implication: Gives the skills a concrete quantity: for each new sub-skill taught, aim for three independent correct solutions before ending the teach block, and count successful spaced re-encounters per topic rather than a single-session percentage. A topic that has reached three correct spaced relearnings is a better definition of examready than one re-test; the tracker's practice runs already carry topic refs and per-item outcomes, so this count could be derived without new fields.

claims.claim: Grade 7 pupils who spread the same maths problems over sessions a week apart scored higher on a later test and judged their own learning more accurately than pupils who did all the problems in one long session, who were overconfident.
claims.source_title: Spaced mathematics practice improves test scores and reduces overconfidence
claims.key_numbers: Grade 7 classroom study; spaced sessions one week apart vs one larger massed session; test-score and prediction-accuracy differences described as substantial and significant; exact figures not shown in search summary
claims.implication: Running two full sessions on the same day (2 Sep) is the massed pattern this study warns against; a second session that day would have been better spent on a different subject or on retrieval of older topics. Because massing inflates confidence, promotion to 'developing' on ~70% supported within the teaching session should be provisional and confirmed in a later session before it counts.

claims.claim: College students with ADHD gain as much from practice testing as students without ADHD: a moderate testing effect in both groups two days later.
claims.source_title: Does Testing Improve Learning for College Students With Attention-Deficit/Hyperactivity Disorder?
claims.key_numbers: n = 25 ADHD, n = 75 non-ADHD college students; two 48-word lists; 8 study trials vs 4 alternating study/test trials; recall test 2 days later; testing effect d = 0.50 and 0.57; testing enhanced both relational and item-specific processing
claims.implication: The retrieval-based design of the starters, exit tickets and the Spanish drills is justified for this student and nothing in the ADHD evidence says retrieval should be replaced by re-teaching. Caveat for the parent: the evidence is from adults learning word lists over a 2-day delay, not 13-year-olds doing GCSE maths.

claims.claim: Retrieval practice works for students with ADHD but does not repair weak initial learning: unmedicated students with ADHD encoded less, used fewer deep strategies and finished lower, while medicated students matched controls.
claims.source_title: Is practice good enough? Retrieval benefits students with ADHD but does not compensate for poor encoding in unmedicated students
claims.key_numbers: All participants benefited from retrieval vs restudy; unmedicated ADHD group worse at encoding and on the final test; medicated group not significantly different from controls; sample sizes and effect sizes not shown in search summary; medication grouping was not randomised. Companion study (Knouse, Rawson & Dunlosky 2020, Learning and Instruction) found ADHD and typically developing students benefited similarly for key-term definitions.
claims.implication: The system's weakest link is the encoding phase, not the testing phase: the teach block must actively secure first learning (worked example, self-explanation prompt, written working every time) because retrieval later will not compensate. Nothing in the tracker or skills records medication status or whether a session fell in a medicated window; the parent should decide privately whether to note this, since it changed outcomes in this study.

claims.claim: Studying worked examples raises maths performance by a medium amount from primary school to adulthood, roughly 18 percentile points, especially when paired with self-explanation prompts.
claims.source_title: A Meta-analysis of the Worked Examples Effect on Mathematics Performance
claims.key_numbers: 8,033 abstracts screened; 43 articles, 55 studies, 181 effect sizes; g = 0.48, p = 0.01; about 18 percentile points; moderators: correct vs incorrect examples, self-explanation prompts, timing (skill acquisition vs practice)
claims.implication: The maths skill's rule 'never give the answer first, one hint at a time' is right for practice but wrong for first teaching of the 24 not-started and 12 gap topics: open each new topic with a fully worked example she must explain back, then a faded example with one step missing (Renkl, Atkinson & Grosse 2004 found learners learn most about the step that is faded), then independent problems. Withdraw the scaffolding as she becomes fluent, because worked examples stop helping once expertise builds (expertise-reversal effect, Sweller, van Merrienboer & Paas 2019).

claims.claim: Children with ADHD show large working-memory deficits in both verbal and visuospatial domains, and the deficit is bigger the more a task loads the central executive.
claims.source_title: Moderators of working memory deficits in children with attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder (ADHD): A meta-analytic review
claims.key_numbers: Large between-group effect sizes across phonological and visuospatial working memory; moderators include central-executive demands, number of trials, recall vs recognition; exact values not shown in search summary
claims.implication: Cognitive-load management matters more for this student than for a typical learner: one instruction per turn, one question part at a time (which also blunts the 'answers every part' habit), written working treated as external memory rather than a compliance rule, and multi-step problems introduced through completion steps. The Spanish Shooting Gallery's speed-up every three correct answers adds time pressure that is extraneous load for vocabulary encoding, so it should stay a consolidation tool for already-known sets, not a first-exposure tool.

caveats: ADHD-specific evidence for durable-learning techniques is thin: the only direct studies found are Knouse and colleagues' work with college students (word lists, key-term definitions, text recall) and Kasper et al. 2012 on working memory in children. No study of spacing, interleaving or worked examples in an ADHD sample was found, and nothing about a 13-year-old home-educated learner; claims C1-C10 and C13 are general-population and their application to this student is inference.

The 2025 maths meta-analysis (Murray, Horner & Goebel) found the testing-vs-restudy effect in maths was not robust (g = 0.18, CI crossing zero), which conflicts with the general testing-effect literature (Adesope 2017; Yang 2021, g = 0.499). Treat retrieval practice in maths as 'do spaced problem-solving' rather than 'quiz on facts'.

The expanding-vs-uniform figure for Latimier et al. 2021 (g = 0.034, non-significant) was reported in a secondary search summary, not in the paper's abstract; the abstract confirms the comparison was made. Kang et al. 2014 (https://link.springer.com/article/10.3758/s13423-014-0636-z) independently found no advantage for expanding schedules at 8 weeks.
Adesope et al. 2017's overall effect size was not visible in any search summary; only the qualitative conclusion is cited.
Emeny, Hartwig & Rohrer 2021 and Rohrer, Dedrick & Stershic 2015: exact score percentages were not shown in search summaries.
Knouse et al. 2023: medication status was a non-randomised grouping, so the medicated/unmedicated difference is observational within an otherwise experimental design.

The Education Endowment Foundation's 2021 evidence review (https://educationendowmentfoundation.org.uk/education-evidence/evidence-reviews/cognitive-science-approaches-in-the-classroom) warns that positive results for spacing, interleaving and retrieval practice mostly come from small or tightly controlled studies and that evidence on applying them across year groups and subjects is limited; this applies doubly to a one-to-one home setting.

Supporting sources named inside implications but without their own claim: Renkl, Atkinson & Grosse 2004 on fading worked steps (https://eric.ed.gov/?id=EJ732331); Sweller, van Merrienboer & Paas 2019 on cognitive load and the expertise-reversal effect (https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s10648-019-09465-5); Janes et al. 2020 on successive relearning in a real course (https://onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/abs/10.1002/acp.3699).

The session's web-search budget was exhausted before three planned searches could run: interleaving in ADHD samples, the result of the 2023 Frontiers study on whole-text vs section free-recall in students with ADHD (https://www.frontiersin.org/journals/psychology/articles/10.3389/fpsyg.2023.1301726/full), and Agarwal et al. 2014 on retrieval practice reducing test anxiety. These remain unconfirmed.

Interval arithmetic in C8 is the agent's calculation from Cepeda et al.'s 5-20% rule applied to the 4 Sep 2026 to 14 May 2027 gap (about 252 days) and an assumed Dec 2026 mock about 100 days away; the optimal gap depends on which test is treated as the target.
